lead: Three fixed windings, fed from a three-phase supply, make a magnetic field that turns at one fixed speed. The rotor has no wire from the supply; the field induces currents in it, and those currents make torque. So the rotor chases the field, always a little slower. That small gap, the slip, controls everything: rotor current, torque, and where the motor settles on the torque-slip curve. Industry runs on this motor: water pumps, fans, lathe spindles, compressors, textile machines.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.2 for induced EMF, and Unit 2 for the three-phase supply and the rotating field.

sections.h3: Stator, rotor and the rotating field

blocks.text: The stator carries a three-phase winding: three coil groups, one per phase, placed 120° apart around the bore. The three phase currents differ in time by 120°, so the three pulsating fluxes add up to one flux of constant magnitude that turns round the bore. This is the rotating field.

The rotor is a cage or a winding. A squirrel-cage rotor is a set of copper or aluminium bars in a laminated iron cylinder, short-circuited at both ends by rings. A wound (slip-ring) rotor carries a real three-phase winding brought out through slip rings and brushes, so external resistance can be added to help starting under heavy load. The cage rotor has no brushes and almost no maintenance, so it drives most pumps, fans, lathes, compressors and textile machines.

blocks.where: N_s is the synchronous speed of the field in rpm; f is the supply frequency in Hz; P is the number of poles of the machine.

blocks.text: The field speed is fixed by supply frequency and pole count. A 4-pole, 50 Hz motor has its field at 1500 rpm whether the shaft is loaded or not.

items: Three-phase currents in three windings set up a flux that rotates at N_s.
The rotating flux cuts the rotor bars and induces an EMF in them (Chapter 3.2).
The bars are shorted by the end rings, so current flows; each current-carrying bar in the field feels a force.
The forces add to a torque that drags the rotor along behind the field.

blocks.text: The rotor never quite catches the field. If it did, the flux would stand still relative to the bars, no EMF would be induced, there would be no rotor current and no torque, and the rotor would slow again. So it settles at a speed N slightly below N_s.

blocks.where: s is the slip, a pure fraction from 0 to 1; N is the rotor speed in rpm; N_s is the synchronous speed in rpm; f_r is the rotor frequency in Hz; f is the supply frequency in Hz.

blocks.text: At standstill N = 0, so s = 1. At full load a typical motor runs at s = 0.02 to 0.05, that is 2% to 5%. A 1500 rpm motor therefore turns at 1425 to 1470 rpm.

The rotor bars see the field slip past at the difference speed, so the induced rotor EMF and current have frequency f_r = s f. At standstill that is the full 50 Hz; at 4% slip it is 2 Hz. Rotor reactance rises with this frequency, X_r = s X_ro, where X_ro is the standstill rotor reactance. That one fact shapes the whole torque curve.
Air-gap power P_ag crosses from stator to rotor through the magnetic field. Torque is that power divided by the speed at which the field delivers it.

blocks.where: T is the torque in N·m; P_ag is the air-gap power in W; ω_s is the synchronous angular speed in rad/s; N_s is in rpm.

blocks.text: At slip s the rotor copper loss is s·P_ag and the mechanical power is (1 − s)·P_ag. Small slip means small loss, which is why the motor is efficient at full load.

At small slip the rotor circuit is almost resistive, so rotor current and torque are both proportional to s: the curve is a straight line from the origin. As slip grows, the rotor reactance s X_ro grows, the rotor current lags further, and each ampere gives less torque. The curve bends over, peaks at the pull-out slip s_m, then falls.

blocks.where: T is torque at slip s; T_max is the peak (pull-out) torque; s_m is the slip at which that peak occurs, typically 0.1 to 0.25.

blocks.text: This is the approximate form; it neglects stator resistance and reactance, so it is accurate near the peak and on the running part of the curve, not at standstill.

On this curve the standstill torque is 0.38 T_max and full load sits at 0.47 T_max, so the starting torque comes to only about 0.8 times full load. A motor like that could not start a loaded pump or hoist. Real cage motors lift the starting point to 1.5 to 2 times full load by using a deep-bar or double-cage rotor, whose resistance is high at standstill and low when running. Pull-out torque is about twice full load, and the motor runs on the near-linear part between no load and full load.

Stability follows from the slope. If the load rises, the rotor slows, slip rises, torque rises, and the motor settles at a new point: this holds for s below s_m. Beyond s_m more slip gives less torque, so the rotor keeps slowing and the motor stalls. That peak is the breakdown torque.

figure.caption: Torque-slip curve from T = 2T_max/(s/s_m + s_m/s) with s_m = 20%. Notice the straight rise near zero slip, the peak of 1.0 per unit at 20% slip, and the fall to about 0.38 per unit at standstill.

spec.aria: Torque rises almost linearly to a peak of 1 per unit at 20 percent slip and then falls to about 0.38 per unit at standstill, 100 percent slip.

examples.question: A 4-pole, 50 Hz, three-phase induction motor runs at 4% slip. Find the synchronous speed, the rotor speed and the rotor frequency. If the air-gap power is 12 kW, find the torque developed.
steps: Synchronous speed: N_s = 120 f / P = 120 × 50 / 4 = 1500 rpm.
Slip is 4%, so s = 0.04. Rotor speed N = N_s (1 − s) = 1500 × 0.96 = 1440 rpm.
Rotor frequency f_r = s f = 0.04 × 50 = 2 Hz.
Synchronous angular speed ω_s = 2π N_s / 60 = 2π × 1500 / 60 = 157.1 rad/s.
examples.answer: N_s = 1500 rpm, N = 1440 rpm, f_r = 2 Hz, and the developed torque is 76.4 N·m.
examples.check:
import math
f = 50.0
P = 4.0
s = 0.04
Pag = 12000.0
Ns = 120 * f / P
N = Ns * (1 - s)
fr = s * f
ws = 2 * math.pi * Ns / 60
T = Pag / ws
print(round(Ns, 1))
print(round(N, 1))
print(round(fr, 1))
print(round(ws, 1))
print(round(T, 1))

traps: Writing s = 4 instead of s = 0.04. Slip is a fraction of synchronous speed, never a percentage inside the formula.
Calling 1440 rpm the synchronous speed. The field always turns at 1500 rpm; only the shaft turns slower.
Using the rotor speed in ω_s when computing torque. T = P_ag/ω_s uses the synchronous angular speed at which the field delivers the power.
Assuming rotor frequency stays at 50 Hz. It is f_r = s f, which falls as the motor speeds up.
Claiming the motor can run at N_s. At N_s there is no relative speed, no rotor EMF, no rotor current, and therefore no torque.

quiz.q: Define slip of a three-phase induction motor and give its value at standstill.
quiz.a: s = (N_s − N)/N_s, where N_s is synchronous speed and N is rotor speed. At standstill N = 0, so s = 1.

quiz.q: A 6-pole induction motor runs on a 50 Hz supply. Find its synchronous speed.
Why can an induction motor never run at synchronous speed?
quiz.a: At N = N_s the field is stationary relative to the rotor, so no EMF is induced, no rotor current flows and no torque is produced. Friction and shaft load then slow the rotor, so it settles below N_s with a small slip.

quiz.q: Why does the torque fall after the pull-out slip even though the rotor current is large?
quiz.a: Rotor reactance s X_ro grows with slip, so the rotor current lags the rotor EMF by a larger angle. The in-phase component of current that produces torque becomes a smaller share of the total, so torque falls.

quiz.q: A 4-pole, 50 Hz induction motor runs at 1440 rpm. Find the slip and the rotor frequency.
A motor driving a pump is loaded until the load torque exceeds the pull-out torque. Describe what happens to the motor.
quiz.a: Slip crosses s_m and torque now falls as slip rises. The rotor decelerates further, slip runs to 1 and the motor stalls. It then draws locked-rotor current, so the winding overheats unless protection trips.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real designs shape the rotor to place the peak where they want it: a deep-bar or double-cage rotor forces current into an outer high-resistance path at starting, giving high starting torque with good running efficiency. Standard designs are grouped into classes A to D by their torque-slip shape, chosen by the load, whether fan, hoist or crusher. Modern practice puts a variable-frequency drive on the stator so the whole curve slides with frequency, which is how pumps and fans are speed-controlled for energy saving. Motor efficiency itself is graded by international efficiency classes. Search for 'double-cage rotor', 'NEMA design classes' and 'V/f control' to go further.
